results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
Repentance - Buße, our word for it - was not one ritual handled by a priest. It was a whole life turned toward God. Our founder's first thesis, the one that began everything in 1517, said exactly this: when our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said "Repent," he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. It had two parts. The first was fear under God's Law, which shows us our sin. The second was trust in his promise, which sets the conscience free. The word came to us from the old church's own practice of penance, where a priest assigned satisfaction for named sins. We kept the word but changed what it named. It was no longer a transaction completed once. It was the shape of a Christian's whole life, lived daily under Law and Gospel.

“They also teach that since Adam's fall, all people conceived in the natural way are born with sin. That is, they are born without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with evil desire. They teach that this disease, or inborn fault, is truly sin. It condemns even now, and it brings eternal death on those not born again through Baptism and the Holy Spirit. They condemn the Pelagians and others who deny that inborn corruption is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, these people argue that a person can be justified before God by his own strength and reason.”

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
Because it was the promise spoken to us from outside, not something we fashioned ourselves. Our founder said plainly: I did nothing; the Word did it all. We believed it because Scripture's own authority was heard again, after it had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching that was not its own. The Word reached us the way it always reaches anyone: preached, taught, and written down, not argued into being by our own effort.

We held Christ's body and blood truly present in the bread and wine because he said so, and we took him at his word. We did not dispute the how. We took our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it. We believed people are saved by faith alone because no other teaching appeared so often in our writings: treatises, sermons, catechisms, and the confession. We could not be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort. We were freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rested on nothing. It clung to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended to Hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person. He bought me and won me from all sins, from death and from the authority of the Devil. It did not cost him gold or silver, but his holy, precious blood, his innocent body -- his death! Because of this, I am his very own. I will live under him in his kingdom. I will serve him in righteousness, innocence and blessedness forever, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

voice_event.text:
Two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels on the first of July, 1523. Theologians from Louvain had pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Word reached our founder within months, and he wrote a ballad about them. It is our one martyr-song. The ballad says they stood firm and were glad to be free of their monks' habits before the fire. It names its own point plainly: by the power of grace they were true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed.

What is documented is two named men and a dated burning. What the ballad adds, such as their exact words and their cheerfulness in that hour, is the song's own voice. It is not an independent witness.

voice_event.text:
That our founder said, more than once, that the Gospel was taught among us and not held. He did not speak of strangers. He spoke of pastors and preachers of our own. In 1522 he told his own Wittenberg congregation that an ass can almost intone the lessons, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. In 1529, in his Large Catechism, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That testimony is his own. It is real, and he gave it more than once. But it is testimony. No report from an actual parish stands beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

Against his prince's wishes, our founder left the Wartburg and returned to a Wittenberg in disorder. He preached eight days running and told his congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform but not yet its love. That was in March 1522. Seven years later, the complaint was sharper still.

At his own table, Katharina asked why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

removed.sentence: "Those who come to the Sacrament must bring with them such a faith and must not doubt that they obtain this treasure. Notice this especially. It is a shame and disgrace that we must drive and force those who want to be Christian to receive such a comfort and treasure, when they should run toward it on their own, and instead have to be urged to it. Do not argue whether you are worthy or not. As I said earlier, God does not offer you comfort and His Sacrament on the basis of your own worthiness. Instead, it is given out of pure mercy, because you are unworthy! Whoever does not desire it and does not feel confident enough to expect His grace, let him be sure that he tempts God and disgraces the Holy Sacrament. For he regards such a comfort and a precious treasure as nothing more than something that could not possibly benefit him. For that reason, the Sacrament should not and cannot be given to such a person."
